# Four Hours Forty-Eight Minutes of Cable

Nayla Wiryawan pulls the Exchange's index one ordinary shift and finds four days of her own life for sale under someone else's name. Lot 4417: twenty-four hours, certified generation 1, detail 0.94, originator Juno Halim — a stranger who now owns four hours forty-eight minutes of memory that came out of Nayla's own skull. The clinic's paper log, written in her own hand, records four "thermal-fault callbacks" she has no memory of authorizing. Her implant holds only ninety days of anything, and the originals are already overwritten; all that survives is a single 36-megabyte fragment, expiring at the next pump siren whether or not she understands what it shows her. In Baruna Reach, where eleven million people live on stilts above their own drowned city and a cheap cortical port is the one thing everyone can afford to sell, experience isn't property — so what was taken from Nayla is, technically, legal. Proving otherwise means proving it happened inside her body, not on a ledger, before her own memory of it disappears for good. Between a dock buyer who signs provenance he doesn't ask about, an assayer who trusts only her bench, and a boat partner who owes debts he can't explain, Nayla has one night and thirty-six megabytes to find out who held her port open — and why. A hard-edged, unsentimental mystery of memory, debt, and drowned infrastructure.

## Comparables

- *Altered Carbon*
- *New York 2140*
- *The Peripheral*
# Chapter 1 — Four Days, Itemised

The index came down at nine kilobits a second, which meant text and nothing else: no thumbnails, no preview trace, just a list building itself a line at a time while the tide worked up the stairwell two flights below.

Lot 4417. Certificate: generation 1, detail 0.94. Originator: Halim, J.

Nayla Wiryawan read the scene titles the way she read a parts manifest, and stopped at the fourth.

*Dawn, Ledge channel, outbound.* *Burn, left wrist, flux spatter.* *Mastoid lead, solder sequence.*

She turned her wrist over. The scar sat where it had always sat, pale against brown, from the morning she had let the iron roll. Nobody else had been on the pontoon. And no one solders a mastoid lead the way she does — shield first, then signal, then the strain loop, because Ilham had taught her that and Ilham had learned it from a man who was dead.

Four days, itemised, under a woman she had never met.

"Twenty-four recorded hours," she said out loud, because a number left unspoken was a number left wrong. "Three-sixty megabytes an hour. Eight thousand six hundred and forty. At half a megabyte a second—" she did it on the bench edge with a fingernail "—four hours forty-eight minutes of cable. Unbroken."

In nine years she had never been out of a chair for four hours and forty-eight minutes at a stretch. Nobody was. The port was a wire behind the ear; a wire behind the ear is a thing people notice.

So it hadn't been one sitting.

The paper log lived under the assay bench, beside the certificate taped to the housing. She went back through it and found the shape of it in four entries, spaced nine days, nine days, eleven.

Day −117. Day −108. Day −99. Day −88.

*Thermal-fault callback. 78 min chair. 4 × 90 s hard-shut. 72 min cable. No charge.*

Identical to the minute. Seventy-two minutes at half a megabyte a second was 2,160 megabytes — six recorded hours, four times over. Her own handwriting, four times over. Dates she remembered arriving at, and not one of them a date she remembered leaving.

Selling the memory wasn't the crime. Nothing about a sold memory had ever been a crime here. The crime was the cable, and the cable was proof, and proof was the one thing she owned.

She queried her own Lattice index over the induction link. Nothing before Day −90; the rolling ninety had eaten it. One fragment survived, stamped Day −88, 36 megabytes. Seventy-two seconds of cable to export. Tension behind her ear. A rig fan. Hands.

Ninety days from Day −88 fell at the 04:00 siren, two days out.

The hull knocked. Ilham Basri came aboard with four fuel cells he had no money for.

"What are you counting?"

"The tide," Nayla said, and closed the log.
# Chapter 2 — The Bench Says Two

The burn on Juno Halim's left wrist was a fact she owned the way she owned the room: four centimetres, pale, from a rig housing that ran hot because someone had bypassed the fan interlock. She knew the smell of it. She could not find the pain.

Ratri Sundoro set the calibration bench on the table and unrolled its certificate, taped to the housing, the way assayers did. "I'll take a sample, not the lot. Twenty-four recorded hours is four hours forty-eight minutes of cable and neither of us has that afternoon. Generation and detail come off six hundred megabytes as well as off the whole file."

"Then take the sample," Juno said.

The bench drew it across the mastoid lead at four megabits, and Juno sat still for it, because six weeks ago she had known how to splice such a lead without ever having been taught, and because that knowledge had begun this week to feel borrowed. Twenty minutes for the sample. Ratri watched the read like a woman watching a kettle.

"Generation two," she said. "Detail zero point eight-eight. Within one percent, and I'll sign it."

Oskar Maas did not move. He had a provenance folder open on his knee and the courtesy of a man who has never once been caught lying.

"The certificate says one," Juno said. "Zero point nine-four."

"The certificate is wrong by one connectome." Ratri turned the display. "Agency markers forged. Rated thirty to sixty days. You're forty-two days in. They're thinning — that's not an opinion, that's the decay curve."

Juno looked at her wrist. Somebody's burn.

"Mr Maas."

"Day minus eighty-six," he said. "Two courier drives at the dock. Generation one, both of them." He turned a page without hurrying. "I opened the provenance under a buyer's name because there was no seller willing to be one. That is permitted. Experience is not property."

"Who brought them?"

"Settlement of a hundred and ninety-four gigabytes of drive stock lost in the Ledge channel. The liability was a technician's, at Estuary Seven." He closed the folder. "I took trace instead of fuel cells. He offered."

The room was very quiet. Two flights below, the tide was doing what it did.

The desk chimed. "A Nayla Wiryawan downstairs," the floor said. "No certificate. Carrying a paper log."

Ratri began, unhurriedly, to repack the bench, and then stopped. "I'll stay," she said. "There's a generation number in dispute."

"There's a woman in dispute," Juno said.

"That isn't assayable."

They went down to meet her, Maas first, the folder under his arm. Juno stayed a moment. On the table lay the certificate: generation 1, detail 0.94, originator Halim. Worth more than the memory it described. Worth more, now, than the memory was true.

She picked it up and put it in her coat.
# Chapter 3 — Seventy-Two Seconds of Cable

Ratri Sundoro set the calibration bench on the pontoon at 22:00, when the pumps took the grid, and stated her terms before she opened the case.

"I certify generation and timestamp. Nothing else. An assay counts brains a file has crossed. It cannot tell me whose life it was." She looked up. "So it has to come out of your port at generation one. Second-hand, it proves nothing and I'll say so."

Nayla had the numbers already. Bench, 140 W. Export head, 90 W. Deck lamp, 30 W: two hundred sixty, under the five-hundred ceiling, on a 4 kWh cell that would carry it past dawn with margin. The transcode rig sat dark under its cover, drawing 900 W when it drew anything, useless tonight and useless to her. She was not copying anything into anyone. She was getting one thing out.

Ilham Basri came aboard at 23:40 to stop it and stayed to explain it, which was worse.

"I kept your connectome map," he said. "From the chair, nine years ago. Nobody thought that strange." He did not sit. "I wrote the thermal-fault protocol. Seventy-eight minutes of chair, four hard-shuts at ninety seconds, seventy-two minutes of cable. Four times. Twenty-four recorded hours." A pause. "I copied your hand into the log because yours was the only hand the log ever held."

"Maas."

"One hundred ninety-four gigabytes of drive stock at the bottom of the Ledge channel. He'd take first generation instead of fuel cells." He looked at the water. "I had nothing else at first generation."

The courier boat came alongside at 02:20, tidal speed, no hurry in it. Juno Halim climbed up with the certificate in a sleeve and handed it over without being asked. The markers had finished decaying. The lot re-flagged in her own skull as somebody else's four days ago, and she had spent those days deciding she would rather be nobody than be Nayla.

Ratri read the certificate, then her own bench log. "Generation one, detail 0.94," she said. "My bench says two and 0.88. That is forged provenance. That is fraud, and Maas's file is in the chain now."

At 03:57 Nayla plugged her own mastoid port, alone, and let it run. Thirty-six megabytes at half a megabyte a second. Seventy-two seconds: cable tension behind the ear, a rig fan, Ilham's hands.

The siren fired at 04:00 and the ninety-day edge took the original mid-breath.

Ilham did not run. The crime had never been in the market.

Nayla wrote the log in her own handwriting — time, megabytes, seconds of cable, no charge — and this time it was true. Everything before that hour was somebody else's copy now, twelve per cent thinner, and nothing would ever put it back.
